etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin convincō (“I refute, prove”), from con- + vincō (“I conquer, vanquish”). Doublet of convict. Displaced native Old English oferreċċan.

definitions.definition: To make someone believe, or feel sure about something, especially by using logic, argument or evidence.

quote.citation: 1718, Francis Atterbury, sermon preached on Easter Day at Westminster Abbey:
quote.text: Such convincing proofs and assurances of it as might enable them to convince others.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene vii], page 135:
quote.text: […] his two Chamberlaines / Will I with Wine, and Waſſell, ſo conuince, / That Memorie, the Warder of the Braine, / Shall be a Fume, […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To confute; to prove wrong.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Atheisme. XVI.”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC, page 90:
quote.text: And therfore, God neuer wrought Miracle, to conuince Atheiſme, becauſe his Ordinary Works conuince it.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To prove guilty; to convict.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, John 8:46, column 1:
quote.text: Which of you conuinceth mee of ſinne?

quote.citation: 1681, John Dryden, The Spanish Fryar: Or, the Double Discovery. […], London:  […]  Richard Tonson and Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act II, page 18:
quote.text: O ſeek not to convince me of a Crime / Which I can ne'er repent, nor can you pardon.
